title: A question about Godard's Historie(s) du Cinema's subtitles

commenti.body:
Yes, that's how I have seen it projected professionally, and how the VHS copies were done. It is really annoying but there's still plenty to gain from the movie, even with the limited subbing. 

I don't have the reference for it but apparently Godard himself supervised the subtitling and translation and chose to prioritize certain sentences and ideas.

It is a very difficult prospect, to provide subtitles for a film that may have three or four images and accompanying audio going at a time.

For Ever Mozart is also subtitled very strangely, but also supervised by Godard. 

[here's an interview he did briefly talking about subtitling (reminder that Bukowski subtitled Every Man for Himself!)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eQQH00Rg-Ds)

This isn't a problem unique to HdC. Godard seems to have a massive problem with specifically English subtitles for some bizarre reason. 

For "Film Socialisme" the only English subtitles available are apparently what he calls "Navajo English" which is a culturally and historically incorrect pidgin language that only emphasizes one or two words per sentence and scraps everything else, making the film near impossible to understand for English subtitle readers.

Godard has made it abundantly clear on multiple occasions that he seems to have a lot of problems with English speaking audiences and that he doesn't make films for them and only tolerates them because it brings wider appeal. ([This academic paper dives into this fairly in depth](https://www.academia.edu/7020895/Against_Translation_Navajo_English_in_Godards_Film_Socialisme)) He strangely did not adopt this approach for other language translations of this film. 

My guess is that the subtitles in HdC are like that entirely on purpose and was his vision for the film.
